newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Food under U.N. plans arrives in northern Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Food under U.N. plans arrives in northern Iraq.

text.p: The first food shipments under an oil-for-food deal have arrived in the Kurdish regions of northern Iraq, more than three months after the programme went into effect, a U.N. official said on Thursday.

Eight trucks carrying 16 metric tons of chickpeas and seven trucks with 109.2 tons of vegetable oil arrived on Wednesday in Zakho in northern Iraq from Turkey where they were bought. The truckloads were part of approved contracts for 6,000 tons of chickpeas and 10,000 tons of vegetable oil.
"So the shipments are still small in volume," said spokesman Juan-Carlos Brandt. "More will arrive later."

Some 13,000 tons of rice from Thailand was expected to arrive at the port of Umm Qasr on March 23, U.N. officials said in an effort to counter a senior Iraqi official's labelling of the plan as the "oil-for-nothing" scheme.
Brandt said the trucks were going to a centre at Ninawa in central Iraq. But he said he did not know how long distributing the supplies would take.

Iraq has been under U.N. sanctions since it invaded Kuwait in August 1990. On Dec. 10, Iraq began to sell oil in order to buy badly-needed supplies for its people under a special Security Council plan that allows $2 billion in oil sales over six months.
A continuing controversy has been the late arrival of the supplies after oil contracts were signed and approved quickly. U.N. oil experts this week approved the 40th crude oil contract for Iraq.
Iraq has blamed the United Nations and the United States for taking too long to approve the contracts while Washington has blamed Iraq.

On Thursday Tareq Aziz, Iraq's deputy prime minister, called the deal the "oil-for-nothing" plan. He told the London-based Arabic newspaper Asharq al-Awsat that not one loaf or bread or tablet of aspirin had arrived yet.
